title: Sāṃkhyakārikā
text:
**SK 1**
Because of the affliction caused by the threefold suffering there arises the desire to know the means of removing it. [If it be objected that] this inquiry is pointless, since perceptible [remedies exist] — [we answer] no, for those [remedies] are not absolute nor lasting.
**SK 2**
The scriptural [remedy] is like the perceptible one, for it is bound up with impurity, decay, and excess [of merit over others]. Superior to both is the [remedy that comes] from the discriminative knowledge of the vyakta / avyakta (the manifest and the unmanifest) and the puruṣa (knower).
**SK 3**
Root nature (prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (primordial material nature)) is uncaused [not a modification of anything]; the seven beginning with mahat / buddhi (the great one) are both cause and effect (prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature-and-modification)); the set of sixteen is [pure] effect (modification); puruṣa (the self) is neither cause nor effect.
**SK 4**
Perception, inference, and trustworthy testimony — since [these] comprise the establishment of every means of knowledge — are held to be the pramāṇa (dṛṣṭa, anumāna, āptavacana) (means of valid knowledge), threefold; for the establishment of what is to be known is [accomplished] through a means of knowledge.
**SK 5**
Perception is the determining of each [sense-]object [as it is grasped]. Inference, declared to be of three kinds, is preceded by [the relation of] the liṅga (mark) and the mark-bearer. Trustworthy testimony is reliable revelation [and reliable report].
**SK 6**
The cognition of things beyond the senses [comes] from inference based on general [observed] correlation. But what is not established even by that — being [wholly] imperceptible — is established from reliable scriptural tradition.
**SK 7**
[A thing may go unperceived] from being too far off, from being too near, from injury to the sense-organ, from inattention of the mind, from subtlety, from intervention [of an obstacle], from being overpowered [by something stronger], and from being mingled with what is similar.
**SK 8**
The non-apprehension of that [unmanifest cause] is due to its subtlety, not to its non-existence; its apprehension is through its effects. And that effect — beginning with mahat / buddhi (the great one) — is both dissimilar to and similar to prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature).
**SK 9**
Because what is non-existent cannot be made [to be]; because [for any effect] a [specific] material cause is required; because everything cannot arise from everything; because a capable [cause] produces only what is possible [to it]; and because [the effect] is of the nature of its cause — therefore the effect pre-exists [in its cause] (satkārya (the effect already real in its cause)).
**SK 10**
The vyakta / avyakta (manifest) is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, mergent [resolvable into its cause], composite, and subordinate. The vyakta / avyakta (unmanifest) is the opposite [of all these].
**SK 11**
Both the manifest and prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (the primary nature) have the three guṇa (sattva, rajas, tamas) (constituent strands), are non-discriminating, are objects [of experience], are common [to all selves], are unconscious, and are productive. puruṣa (The self), however, is the opposite of these.
**SK 12**
The guṇa (sattva, rajas, tamas) (guṇas) have the natures of pleasure, pain, and dejection respectively; they serve the purposes of illumination, activity, and restraint; and their modes of operation are mutual domination, mutual support, mutual production, and mutual coupling.

title: Sāṃkhyakārikā
text:
**SK 13**
Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas to be stimulating and mobile; tamas verily to be heavy and enveloping. Their functioning, [though their natures conflict,] is for a [single] purpose, like [the parts of] a lamp.
**SK 14**
That [the manifest] is non-discriminating and the rest is established by [its] having the three guṇas, and by the absence [in it] of what is contrary to this. And because the effect is of the nature of the qualities of its cause, the vyakta / avyakta (unmanifest) too is [thereby] established [as triguṇa].
**SK 15**
Because distinct things are [finite and] measured; because of [their] homogeneity [pointing to a common source]; because [effects] proceed from [the cause's] potency; because of the distinction between cause and effect; and because of the non-distinction [merging] of the entire manifold [at dissolution] —
**SK 16**
— [therefore] the vyakta / avyakta (unmanifest) cause exists. It operates through the three guṇa (sattva, rajas, tamas) (guṇas) and through their commingling [and] by transformation, like water [taking on different forms], according to the distinctions [arising] from the particular dominance of each respective guṇa.
**SK 17**
Because every aggregate exists for another's sake; because there must be something contrary to [that which has] the three guṇas and the rest; because there must be a [conscious] superintendent; because there must be an experiencer; and because activity tends toward kaivalya (isolation) — [therefore] the puruṣa (self) exists.
**SK 18**
Because birth, death, and the [bodily] instruments are severally allotted [to each]; because activity is not simultaneous [in all]; and because the proportions of the three guṇas vary [from one to another] — the plurality of puruṣa (selves) is established.
**SK 19**
And from that contrariety [of the self to nature] it is established that this puruṣa (self) is a witness, and possesses isolation, neutrality, the role of mere seer, and non-agency.
**SK 20**
Therefore, through that conjunction [of the two], the unconscious liṅga (mark-body) appears as if conscious; and likewise, though agency belongs to the guṇa (sattva, rajas, tamas) (guṇas), the indifferent [self] appears as if it were the agent.
**SK 21**
For the puruṣa (self)'s sake of seeing [nature] and for prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (the primary nature)'s sake of [bringing about the self's] kaivalya (isolation), the conjunction of the two [occurs] — as of a lame man and a blind man; and from it [arises] creation.
**SK 22**
From prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature) [arises] mahat / buddhi (the great one); from that, the ahaṃkāra (I-maker); from that, the set of sixteen; and from five of that set of sixteen [arise] the five gross elements.
**SK 23**
mahat / buddhi (Intellect) is [marked by] determination. [Its] virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and lordliness — these are its sāttvika form; the reverse of these is [its] tāmasa form.
**SK 24**
The ahaṃkāra (I-maker) is self-conceit. From it a twofold creation proceeds: the set of eleven [organs], and the fivefold set of tanmātra (subtle elements).
**SK 25**
The sāttvika set of eleven proceeds from the modifying (guṇa (sattva, rajas, tamas) (vaikṛta)) ahaṃkāra (I-maker); the tanmātra (subtle elements) [proceed] from the elemental [tāmasa] I-maker, the source of the elements; and both [proceed] by [the impetus of] the taijasa [rajasic I-maker].
**SK 26**
The cognitive organs are called eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin. Voice, hands, feet, the organ of excretion, and the generative organ they call the action-organs.

title: Sāṃkhyakārikā
text:
**SK 27**
Among these, the mind partakes of the nature of both [classes of organ]; it is the deliberating [faculty], and is also a sense-organ because of its shared characteristics [with them]. Their manifoldness, and the variety of external things, arise from the particular transformations of the guṇa (sattva, rajas, tamas) (guṇas).
**SK 28**
The function of the five [cognitive organs] with regard to sound and the rest [their objects] is held to be bare awareness; and [the functions] of the five [action-organs] are speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and [generative] enjoyment.
**SK 29**
The function of the three [internal organs — intellect, I-maker, mind] is [each] their own distinctive [function], and this is particular to each. Their common function [of the instrument as a whole] is the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa (breath).
**SK 30**
With regard to a present object, the function of the four [intellect, I-maker, mind, and a single sense] is declared [to occur] both simultaneously and successively; but with regard to an unperceived [past or future] object, the function of the three [internal organs] is preceded by that [perception].
**SK 31**
[The organs] each undertake their own function, prompted by mutual intention [to cooperate]. The puruṣa (self)'s purpose alone is the [final] motive; the instrument is not made to act by anything [external to nature's own purposiveness].
**SK 32**
The instrument is of thirteen kinds; it carries [in objects], holds [them], and illuminates [them]. Its effect [the operation upon objects] is tenfold: what is carried, what is held, and what is illuminated.
**SK 33**
The internal instrument is of three kinds; the external is tenfold, [serving] as the object-field of those three. The external instrument [operates in] the present time; the internal instrument [operates in] all three times.
**SK 34**
Of these, the five cognitive organs have for their objects [things both] specific and non-specific [gross and subtle]. Speech has sound for its object; the remaining [action-organs] have the five [gross objects] for their fields.
**SK 35**
Since mahat / buddhi (the intellect), together with the [other two] internal organs, penetrates every object, therefore the threefold [internal] instrument is the doorkeeper, and the remaining [external organs] are the doors.
**SK 36**
These [organs], like lamps, mutually distinct [yet cooperating], being particular modifications of the guṇa (sattva, rajas, tamas) (guṇas), illuminate the whole object [meant] for the puruṣa (self) and present it to the mahat / buddhi (intellect).
**SK 37**
Since it is the mahat / buddhi (intellect) that accomplishes for the puruṣa (self) the full experience of everything, it is also that same [intellect] which discriminates the subtle distinction between prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (the primary nature) and the self.
**SK 38**
The tanmātra (subtle elements) are the non-specific [aviśeṣa]; from these five [arise] the five gross elements. These [gross elements] are called the specific [viśeṣa]: tranquil, turbulent, and deluding.
**SK 39**
The specific [bodies] are threefold: the subtle [bodies], those born of mother and father, together with the gross elements. Of these, the subtle ones are permanent [persisting through transmigration], while those born of mother and father perish.
**SK 40**
Produced before [the gross body], unattached, fixed [enduring], extending from mahat / buddhi (the great one) down to the subtle elements, devoid of experience [in itself], perfumed by the bhāva (dispositions) — the liṅga (mark-body) transmigrates.

title: Sāṃkhyakārikā
text:
**SK 41**
Just as a picture [cannot exist] without a support, and just as a shadow [cannot exist] without a post and the like, so without the specific [gross bodies] the liṅga (mark-body) cannot subsist, support-less.
**SK 42**
Motivated by the puruṣa (self)'s purpose, through the connection of cause [the dispositions] and effect [transmigration], and by virtue of prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature)'s pervasive power, the liṅga (mark-body) performs [its many roles], like an actor.
**SK 43**
The bhāva (dispositions) beginning with virtue are seen [to be of three kinds]: innate, derived from nature, and acquired [by modification]; they rest upon the instrument [the intellect], while [their effects], beginning with the embryo, rest upon the [bodily] effect.
**SK 44**
By virtue [comes] ascent upward; by vice [comes] descent downward; by knowledge [comes] release; and by the reverse [of knowledge, i.e. error] bondage is held [to result].
**SK 45**
From dispassion [comes] absorption into prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature); from rajasic attachment comes transmigration; from lordliness [comes] unobstructedness; and from the reverse [of lordliness] comes the reverse of that [obstruction].
**SK 46**
This is the pratyaya-sarga (intellectual creation), named [under the four heads of] viparyaya / aśakti / tuṣṭi / siddhi (error, disability, contentment, and attainment); arising from the disequilibrium and clash of the guṇa (sattva, rajas, tamas) (guṇas), its subdivisions are fifty.
**SK 47**
The subdivisions of error are five; those of disability, [arising] from defect of the instruments, are twenty-eight; contentment is ninefold; and attainment is eightfold.
**SK 48**
The subdivision of obscurity (tamas) is eightfold; of delusion (moha) [also eightfold]; great delusion (mahā-moha) is tenfold; gloom (tāmisra) is eighteenfold; and so likewise is blinding gloom (andha-tāmisra).
**SK 49**
The injuries to the eleven organs, together with the injuries to the mahat / buddhi (intellect), are declared to be disability (viparyaya / aśakti / tuṣṭi / siddhi (aśakti)); the seventeen injuries to the intellect [arise] from the failure [the reverse] of contentment and attainment.
**SK 50**
Four [contentments] are internal, named after prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature), [the right] means, time, and good fortune; and five are external, [arising] from abstention from [the five] objects [of sense]. Thus nine contentments (viparyaya / aśakti / tuṣṭi / siddhi (tuṣṭi)) are held.
**SK 51**
Reasoning, [oral] instruction, study, the three [kinds of] removal of suffering, the gaining of [good] friends, and [pure] giving — [these are] the eight attainments (viparyaya / aśakti / tuṣṭi / siddhi (siddhi)). The threefold [hindrance] preceding [these] attainments is the goad [namely error, disability, and contentment].
**SK 52**
Without the bhāva (dispositions) there is no liṅga (mark-body), and without the mark-body there is no accomplishment of the dispositions. Hence a twofold creation proceeds: the one called the [creation of the] mark-body and the one called the [creation of the] dispositions.
**SK 53**
The divine [order] is of eight varieties; the animal kind is fivefold; and the human is of a single kind. Such, in brief, is the elemental creation.
**SK 54**
Above, the creation abounds in sattva; below, at the base, it abounds in tamas; in the middle, it abounds in rajas — [this holds] from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
**SK 55**
Therein the conscious puruṣa (self) undergoes the suffering wrought by old age and death, so long as the liṅga (mark-body) does not cease. Therefore suffering is, by [its very] nature, [inherent in embodied existence].

title: Sāṃkhyakārikā
text:
**SK 56**
Thus this undertaking, wrought by prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature), extending from mahat / buddhi (the great one) down to the specific [gross] elements, is [carried out] for the sake of the liberation of each puruṣa (self) — for another's sake, [though performed] as if for nature's own.
**SK 57**
Just as the [unconscious] flow of milk serves for the nourishment of the calf, so the activity of prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (the primary nature) serves for the liberation of the puruṣa (self).
**SK 58**
Just as people engage in actions in order to relieve [their] restless longing, so the vyakta / avyakta (unmanifest) engages [in activity] for the sake of the liberation of the puruṣa (self).
**SK 59**
As a dancer, having shown herself to the audience, withdraws from the dance, so prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature), having revealed herself to the puruṣa (self), withdraws.
**SK 60**
By manifold means [nature], being possessed of qualities, acts benevolently — without [any return of] benefit — for the sake of the self, who is quality-less and confers no benefit [on her]; [she acts] for his sake, though [it brings] no purpose [of her own].
**SK 61**
"There is nothing more delicate [modest] than prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature)" — such is my conviction; for [thinking] "I have been seen," she never again comes within the sight of the puruṣa (self).
**SK 62**
Therefore, in truth, no [self] whatever is bound, nor liberated, nor does it transmigrate. It is prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature), in its manifold supports [bodies], that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated.
**SK 63**
By seven forms [virtue, vice, ignorance, dispassion, lordliness, and their opposites] prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature) binds herself by herself; and that same [nature], for the puruṣa (self)'s sake, frees [herself] by one form [namely true knowledge].
**SK 64**
Thus, through repeated meditation on the principles [there arises the realization]: "I am not [an agent], nothing is mine, [this is] not-I" — complete, free from error, pure, and absolute knowledge arises.
**SK 65**
By that [knowledge] the puruṣa (self) beholds prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (nature), who has ceased to produce and, her purpose [accomplished], has withdrawn from the seven forms — [he beholds her] poised like a spectator, fully at ease.
**SK 66**
"I have seen [her]" — so [thinks] the one [self], indifferent; "I have been seen" — so the other [nature] desists. Though the conjunction of the two still persists, there is no [further] purpose for creation.
**SK 67**
Upon the attainment of right knowledge, when virtue and the rest [the dispositions] become incapable of being a cause [of rebirth], [the self] continues to bear the body by the force of [past] momentum, like the spinning of a [potter's] wheel.
**SK 68**
When the separation from the body is attained, and prakṛti / pradhāna / mūlaprakṛti (the primary nature) ceases, its purpose having been fulfilled, [the self] attains kaivalya (isolation) that is both absolute and final.
**SK 69**
This secret knowledge of the puruṣa (self)'s purpose was fully expounded by the supreme sage [Kapila] — [the teaching] wherein the persistence, origination, and dissolution of beings are considered.
**SK 70**
This pure and foremost [knowledge] the sage [Kapila] gave out of compassion to Āsuri; Āsuri [gave it] in turn to Pañcaśikha, by whom the doctrine (saptati / Ṣaṣṭitantra (tantra)) was made manifold [widely expanded].

title: Sāṃkhyakārikā
text:
**SK 71**
[The doctrine] handed down through the succession of disciples — this was condensed into āryā verses by the noble-minded Īśvarakṛṣṇa, having rightly understood the established conclusion (satkārya (siddhānta)). [A transmission verse, uncommented by Gauḍapāda.]
**SK 72**
The topics that are in the saptati / Ṣaṣṭitantra (Seventy) are indeed the [whole] topics of the entire Ṣaṣṭitantra ["Sixty-topic system"], [but] devoid of illustrative tales and free also of [the refutation of] rival doctrines. [A transmission verse, uncommented by Gauḍapāda; Paramārtha notes it is not original.]
**SK 73**
Therefore this treatise, [though] seen in brief, is not deficient in meaning — like the reflection [transferred] into a mirror of the vast-bodied [original] doctrine. [Non-canonical appendix: this verse occurs only in V1 and M, after the word "samāptam" ("completed"); excluded from the canonical seventy.]
